content: Israel's approach to animal welfare is governed by the Animal Welfare Law of 1994, which is divided into two main components: the Animal Protection Law and the Animal Experimentation Law. This legislation was introduced by Abraham Poraz and was officially passed by the Knesset on January 11, 1994. Additional regulations under the Animal Protection Law include the establishment of the Animal Welfare Fund in 1995 and the introduction of permit requirements for organizing animal exhibitions and competitions in 2001. Israel also has four other laws related to animal welfare: the Wildlife Protection Law of 1955, the Animal Disease Ordinance of 1985, the Dog Regulation Law of 2002, and the Rabies Regulations (Vaccinations) of 2005. The Minister of Agriculture in Israel is responsible for enforcing the Animal Welfare Law, while the Minister of the Environment appoints trustees to file complaints against offenders. The law also created the Animal Welfare Fund, which supports education, public awareness, and assistance to animal welfare organizations. Between 2005 and 2006, 5 million NIS (approximately $782,000 or €616,500) were allocated to animal welfare initiatives. These projects included education programs, the appointment of animal welfare trustees, efforts to reduce stray animal populations, promotion of animal adoption, assistance to the Israel Police, responses to public requests for help with animals in distress, and support for animal welfare organizations. The Animal Experimentation Law regulates the use of animals in research and established a 23-member National Council for Animal Experimentation. This council has the authority to prohibit animal use in experiments if a reasonable alternative exists. However, animal rights groups, such as CHAI (Concern for Helping Animals in Israel), argue that alternatives are rarely explored adequately and that the law primarily protects the interests of researchers, pharmaceutical companies, and the government rather than the animals themselves. The council mandates that the smallest number of animals be used in experiments and that animal suffering be minimized. Researchers are required to complete courses in animal care, and surprise inspections of research facilities are conducted to ensure compliance. The Wildlife Protection Law of 1955 aligns with the standards of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and prohibits hunting wild animals using traps, snares, nets, or poisons. The Dog Regulation Law of 2002 mandates licenses for all dogs aged three months or older, requires microchip implants, and enforces routine rabies vaccinations. It also regulates the import and ownership of dangerous dog breeds. The Rabies Regulations of 2005 further address vaccination requirements. In 1994, a new law enforcement policy was introduced to combat animal cruelty, instructing police stations to investigate reports of abuse. An educational program was also launched in schools, proposing a one-hour weekly class discussion on animal welfare. Israel has implemented several bans to protect animals. These include prohibiting the dissection of animals in elementary and secondary schools (with optional participation allowed at the university level), banning performances by trained animals in circuses, and outlawing the production of foie gras. The foie gras ban is particularly notable, as Israel was once the fourth-largest producer of foie gras globally but ceased production for ethical reasons. Additionally, the state prohibits killing animals with poison, forcing unfit animals to work, and overworking animals to the point of exhaustion. Although Israel has never had a whaling industry, it joined the International Whaling Commission to vote against the resumption of commercial whaling. In May 2001, eight alleged animal rights activists sent a death threat via fax to immunologist and former dean Shraga Segal of Ben Gurion University’s medical school. This occurred after Segal appeared on a television talk show discussing animal experimentation alongside Likud party member Dani Naveh. Segal, a member of the National Council for Animal Experimentation, opposed Naveh's proposal to increase the number of animal rights activists on the council. At the time, activists represented only three out of the council's 23 academic members. Naveh advocated for expanding their representation to one-third or even half of the council.
